_pattern_report: Yes, a cross-item pattern felt exploitable, though it is semantic rather than positional or length-based. Option lengths looked deliberately balanced (several items had a long distractor, e.g. 3C, 5C, 18B, 22D, so the old longest-is-key tell did not decide my picks), and my letters spread across all four slots without obvious clustering. What did feel exploitable is a shared answer TEMPLATE: on nearly every purpose/structure/main-idea item the winner is the 'qualified reframe' option — the one that complicates, recasts, or adds a contingency to a received view (5A, 16A, 17C, 19C, 21D, 22C, 23D, 24D, and arguably 7D, 13C, 18A). Once I noticed it around item 5, I could pick most later rhetorical items in seconds by scanning for the hedged both-sides option, without any content reasoning. A secondary, milder tell: absolutes ('only', 'invariably', 'no role at all', 'regardless') mark distractors so consistently that eliminating them usually left one or two candidates. The evidence/strengthen items (2, 6, 9, 10, 14, 15, 20) felt genuinely content-dependent and were my least confident guesses.
